newsitem.title: ITALY: MOTOR RACING-IMOLA ASKS HOW `KING SENNA' DIED.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-IMOLA ASKS HOW `KING SENNA' DIED.

text.p: Ayrton Senna's memory lives on in this small Italian backwater, almost three years after the brilliant Brazilian driver died in a high-speed crash at the nearby racing circuit.

Next to the spot where the triple world champion lost control of his Formula One car, people still come to lay bunches of fresh flowers and one fan has painted the words "Someone killed the King" on a nearby wall.

Prosecutors have charged six men, including Williams team boss Frank Williams, with manslaughter in connection with Senna's death, and their long-awaited trial opened on Thursday in a converted ballroom.

A handful of fans wearing Senna memorabilia showed up for the first session and a man stood in silence at the entrance of the makeshift coutroom holding up a picture of the young Brazilian with the words "tell us the truth" written alongside.
Before Judge Antonio Costanzo could get down to the serious business of finding out what happened at the fateful 1994 San Marino Grand Prix, he first had to deal with the world's media.

Authorities decided to hold the trial in the dance hall, which still has disco lights attached to the walls, to have enough room for the hordes of reporters accredited for one of the most sensational cases in motor racing history.

But Costanzo, with the sign "The Law is Equal for Everyone" written above his head, was not prepared to turn his ballroom court into a media circus and swiflty ordered the massed ranks of cameramen and photographers out of the sunny hall.

Only one of the defendants showed up for the opening day, but the front of the court was packed with lawyers, wearing their traditional tassled robes, coming up to chat with journalists and explain the complexities of Italian law.
"I've never seen anything like it," said one radio reporter from the BBC, used to the more sedate world of British justice.
Nor had Imola, whose narrow, colonaded streets were invaded by television satellite trucks.
Solicitor Cosetta Colletti hurled abuse at one van, whose humming generator was parked beneath her office, and threatened to call the police unless the machine was switched off.
A group of pensioners at the Imola social centre, which is hosting the trial, also had their doubts.

"Senna's death will be remembered here forever, it was an appalling day," said Maria Grazia, sitting in a bar below the courtroom. "But we hope all this racket goes away soon and we can get our dance hall back".
She will probably be disappointed. Italian justice is notoriously slow and with only two sessions planned a week, the Senna trial is expected to last several months.
After the bustle of the law court, the Imola circuit was eerily quiet.
The notorious Tamburello curve, where 32-year-old Senna crashed, has now been dismantled, but the place has become a shrine, drawing motor enthusiasts from around the world.
Next to the fencing beside the track, someone has brought a large marble gravestone, written in German, which says simply: "In remembrance of Ayrton Senna".
